text.0_Introduction, 0_Paragraph: The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 3 of Shemonah Perakim, and these are his words: “The ancients said that the soul has health and illness just as the body has health and illness. The health of the soul is that its disposition should be such… that it continually performs good and proper deeds. And its illness is that its disposition should be such… that it continually performs bad and disgraceful deeds. And just as those with bodily illnesses, when they become aware of their sickness, ask the physicians who inform them of what they must do and warn them accordingly…, so too, those whose souls are ill must seek out the sages, who are the physicians of the soul…, and they will heal them through the practices by which the dispositions of the soul are healed…”— so far are his words; see there. And likewise the Rambam wrote in Chapter 2 of Hilchot De’ot, relating the illness of the soul to the illness of the body; see there.
text.0_Introduction, 1_Paragraph: And behold, just as in the processes of the body’s wellbeing—its vitality, its health, and its structure—it is already known that over the course of generations, human strength continually declines, until in our generation, due to our many sins, health has diminished and weakness has increased. Illness and pain, of every affliction and every disease, affect a great number of people. So too is it with the processes of the soul’s wellbeing: the life of the spirit does not remain firm in its place. Generation after generation, the spiritual condition has declined; the health of the soul diminishes, and those stricken and afflicted with the sickness of the soul grow ever more numerous with time.
text.0_Introduction, 2_Paragraph: Indeed, in earlier generations, it was only over the course of an entire generation—from fathers to grandchildren—that a shift could be felt in the state of Torah and reverence when compared with the preceding generation. But now, in this last generation, alas, due to our many sins, within the span of but a few short years, a new spirit passes over the face of the people. It carries upon its wings a multitude of changes, an endless host of transformations. Already one can see and sense a great alteration: a deepening weakness and enfeeblement of the soul in matters of Torah, reverence, and the service of the Blessed One. These go on steadily diminishing, until this dark hour in which the sicknesses of the soul have encompassed almost all flesh—may God have mercy.
text.0_Introduction, 3_Paragraph: And when we look with discerning eyes upon the state of Torah and reverence in general, to see in which of them the sickness of the soul has prevailed more grievously, it is plain to the eye that there is no comparison between the weakness of Torah and the frailty of reverence. For behold, despite all the tribulations that have befallen our holy Torah—its diminished esteem and the desolation of its gates—nevertheless, the promise of the Giver of the Torah, blessed be His Name, remains steadfast: that the testimony shall not be forgotten from the mouth of the seed of Jacob. This has sustained us even to this very day. For the voice, the voice of Jacob (Gen. 27:22), is still heard in the houses of study, and the gates of Zion, distinguished by the learning of halachah, are wide open. And thus there are found, blessed be the Lord, pure-hearted ones who support it with in their decisions and their responses.
text.2_, 6_Chapter, 2_Paragraph: Now let us return and see what would be the first cause to have a person be aroused to examine his actions and meditate introspectively during the month of Elul (this matter is relevant to the whole year, in that it touches upon His service, may His name be blessed) - is it not the case that he has no natural desire for this, as [he does] with earthly matters? Our early rabbis - Eden is their rest - trembled about this thing. They relied upon the Pirkei deRabbi Eliezer and instituted the blowing of the shofar in Elul; and it became the first cause for someone to be aroused from his sleep and from the vanities of his slumbers to examine his actions. It is like the statement of the verse (Amos 3:6), "When a ram’s horn is sounded in a town, do the people not tremble?"
text.2_, 6_Chapter, 3_Paragraph: However it is known that an effect is only created by a cause similar to it. A weighty effect will not come out of a light cause!
text.2_, 6_Chapter, 4_Paragraph: And with this thing, the blowing of the shofar was the first cause for someone who was immersed, both inside and out, in His service, may His name be blessed. So a light cause could arouse him to examine himself in a more lofty way. But what can we say or speak? What can be done now when we are immersed, both inside and out, in the the vanities of earthly pursuits, and the heart is blocked and as hard as a solid boulder? Will the light arousal [of the shofar] in front of us make an impression upon the powerful rock?
text.2_, 27_Chapter, 8_Paragraph: And that is why when they prayed for rain: Behold Rabbi Akiva's approach was like the way of Hilllel, to forego his reckonings [with others for their sins against him]. Hence he was answered from the Heavens measure for measure. However Rabbi Eliezer's approach was like the way of Shammai, so he would not forego his reckonings. Though it is true that he would receive much reward  about this - that which he did the will of God, may His name be blessed, according to his position; nevertheless, since he ultimately would not forego his reckonings, [for the Heavens to] forego the sins of the community would not have been measure for measure. And that is why he was not answered. So this is the meaning of the heavenly voice which said, "It is not because this one is greater than that one, but rather because this one forgoes his reckonings, etc." That is why he was answered, measure for measure, as just mentioned.
